utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is case number IT-02-60-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: May we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Peter McCloskey for the Office of the Prosecutor with Stefan Waespi, Anne Davis, and Janet Stewart, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Nikolic is represented by me, Veselin Londrovic, and Mr. Kirsch; and Mrs. Vesna Anic is our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you understand? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain at this stage? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you have any problems in following the proceedings, just let us know. THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Well, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. During the Pre-Trial Conference, I understand Mr. Nikolic and his lead counsel was absent. Let me introduce the Bench to you once again. Sitting on my right is Judge Vassylenko from the Ukraine; sitting on my left is Judge Argibay from Argentina, and my name is Liu Daqun, the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber I. This Trial Chamber is seized with a joint motion for consideration of plea agreement between Momir Nikolic and the Office of the Prosecutor. This motion was filed jointly by counsel for Mr. Nikolic and the Prosecution on 6 May 2003. According to the plea agreement attached to the joint motion, the accused Nikolic agrees to plead guilty to count 5 of the amended joint indictment, dated the 27th May 2002, as a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(H) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The plea agreement contains provisions reflecting the understanding of the accused Nikolic as to the nature of count 5, including legal elements of persecution as a crime against humanity and the factual basis agreed upon as the basis for his guilty plea to the count. The plea agreement also recommends a range of sentences, based on the understanding that such recommendation is not binding on the Trial Chamber. The Office of the Prosecutor agrees to move to dismiss, at the time of sentencing, the remaining charges set out in the indictment. The Trial Chamber has observed that the plea agreement has also been in the B/C/S language, which the accused Nikolic understands, and is attached to the joint motion. The Trial Chamber also looked at provisions of the relevant Rules, in particular Rule 62 ter, and will deal with the proceedings under Rule 62 bis. Since we just got this plea agreement, could we ask both parties to brief us on this agreement. Then we might ask some questions to both parties. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could take the lead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is a standard form plea agreement that is specifically adapted to this case that counsel for Nikolic and the Prosecutor worked a long time to -- to get. It basically is designed as a document to make sure that the parties understand each other and that -- especially that Mr. Nikolic understands the nature and consequences of the charges, the potential consequences of the plea, and the promises of the Prosecution, the most important of which are that these are recommendations only, as you have stated, and that the Court is of course not bound by this agreement and that you are free, at the time of sentencing, to do so as you wish within the Statute. And as it's pointed out in the plea agreement, that Mr. Nikolic could face up to life imprisonment on this, and that has been explained, I know, in the plea agreement and I know by counsel of the -- for the accused, but that the Prosecution has promised to recommend 15 to 20 years, and also Mr. Nikolic has promised to cooperate and testify at any Srebrenica trials. And these are the -- the basics of the plea agreement, to ensure that Mr. Nikolic understands what he is facing by doing this, understands what the Prosecution is recommending and what his own counsel are recommending. And I -- from my dealings with counsel, I believe that there are no -- no misunderstandings, no problems, no issues that we're aware of and that all of us are going into this freely and voluntarily. And I can ask -- of course answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any observations or submissions from the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully second all that Mr. McCloskey, my learned friend from the Prosecution, has just said. Mr. Kirsch and I have explained in detail to our client, Mr. Nikolic, all the items of the agreement. We have briefed him about the nature of that crime, the crime against humanity, that is, persecutions, which he will plead guilty for today. We are quite sure that Mr. Nikolic has understood all the items of the agreement, and there are no salient questions or any misunderstandings between the Defence and the Prosecution, as my learned colleague has already pointed out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My question to you is that do you understand, fully understand, this plea agreement? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we will ask some questions. My first question is addressed to the Prosecution: Does the Prosecution seek to separate the case of Mr. Nikolic from the other three accused in the case IT-02-60-PT?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be our intention and the intention of the parties that once Mr. Nikolic pleads guilty and that -- that that plea is accepted by this Court, that he would thereby be convicted of these charges and would be, in that sense, no longer a part of the ongoing case. And this is the traditional method, and it's a self-fulfilling procedure. Once one admits guilt, he is convicted and then set down for sentencing, and that he of course is no longer part of the ongoing case which the others are challenging and standing on their right to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some specific questions concerning with the whole plea agreement. We will ask these questions I think paragraph by paragraph. In paragraph 4(b), it says: "That the Office of the Prosecutor agrees to move to dismiss at time of sentencing the remaining charges set out in the Indictment." What does it mean? What is the time of the sentencing? What is the remaining charges set out in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, what -- that is again a traditional part of a plea agreement in -- both in this Tribunal and other places, and what it means is that at the time Mr. Nikolic is sentenced, at that sentencing hearing and at the time of sentence, the Prosecution will move to dismiss all the other charges. It's done in a -- sort of an oddly conservative fashion, as you -- as you might view it, but sometimes in the common law system between a plea and an actual sentence an accused may wish to challenge his guilty plea. And in that case, if the Prosecution has already dismissed the charges, then they many times cannot be reinstituted in a common law jurisdiction. So this is just a means by which to ensure that we get to the state of sentencing, that it -- it goes through as anticipated by the plea agreement, and then the other charges -- the other counts in the indictment, in this case, are dismissed and go away. In this plea agreement, we are -- Mr. Nikolic has agreed to testify in the upcoming trial, and we have requested that his sentencing be set for after his testimony so that the Court can fully evaluate his -- his testimony and his overall contribution to the Prosecution's case, which is part of the foundation of why the Prosecution has agreed to drop the other charges and make this sentence recommendation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You use the terminology of "standard traditions." Traditionally, you know, this is the normal practice, you know. I would like to know, you know, from the previous practice or from previous cases whether this is really something, you know, in the plea agreement or not. Can you cite some previous cases on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's hard to use the word "tradition" when it comes to this Tribunal, since we haven't been around very long. But in the sense that we can say "tradition," I was personally involved in the plea agreement of Drazen Erdemovic, a soldier, that was -- actually pled guilty to charges in this case, and that plea agreement was designed on very -- very similar format than this one. And in fact, the first time Mr. Erdemovic pled guilty, it was such a different -- a different and unusual plea in a situation -- I recall at the time Judge Jorda was presiding and there was some confusion, and later on it was not clear that Mr. Erdemovic understood his rights and that had to be done all over again. And the second time it was done, I was involved and we were able to make an actual written plea agreement much along the lines of this one, and I think it was then much clearer to -- to Mr. Erdemovic, much clearer to counsel, much clearer to the Court, and eventually that was upheld. So that is one situation. Another situation was in the case of accused Milan Simic, who was in the Bosanski Samac case, who was one of four defendants, who a few months ago now pled guilty pursuant to a plea agreement which was, again, based on the very same design as this standard form, and that has withstood the test of the Tribunal. And while I have not carefully reviewed the Plavsic plea agreement, it is also, in my understanding, a similar -- a similar agreement, though drafted by other lawyers so perhaps a little different. But those are three examples of the traditions within this Tribunal. And I believe it was the Erdemovic case that caused the Tribunal to recognise that this was something that is important, and so it became the subject of one of the plenaries and the Judges did adopt the section that did recognise the validity of such agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, as we understand it, the practice of the Tribunal, which is common with many of the domestic jurisdictions, is to sentence the accused before he gives any evidence. This avoids any suggestion that he's inflated or invented his evidence which is given in order to obtain a great reduction for mitigation of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the -- the practice in the -- in North America, and not to say that any one system is any better than any others, is a very practical system, and what both the Prosecution and the Defence want in a plea agreement is a chance for the accused, or the guilty party, to testify as truthfully and as completely as possible and show the Trial Chamber who will be gauging his cooperation and his truthfulness that he is fully complying with his agreement and with his promise to tell the truth. And the most important act that that person can do is testify under oath before the Tribunal. So I think you will find that all Defence counsel will want their clients to be -- not be sentenced until after they have a chance to testify under oath to show the Judges that they are truly cooperating, that they have truly accepted their responsibility, and they're not playing games. Because as you know, Courts in this Tribunal have said repeatedly that people that accept their responsibility and admit the truth of the charges and save the victims from testifying and save the court time, that that is something that is strongly recommended. And so accused will want to be able to show the Court that there -- that they are truthful, that they are accepting their responsibility, and the best way for them to do that is under cross-examination by any other co-accused and by questions from the Court. Now, of course the Court has every right and can question an accused at the sentence to ensure themselves that the plea is factual, based on facts, and is also voluntary. And that is your duty. But there is nothing like testimony and the cross-examination. This is where the accused has a real chance to show you his honesty, show you his -- his acceptance of responsibility. And there's also one very practical reason why this happens: Is that if an accused is sentenced prior to giving testimony, the accused may feel that he can say anything he wants afterward and there is no -- there is no -- nothing to make him live up to his agreement. And this is perhaps the sense that you feel that there's a sense of coercion about the process, and that is the nature of the process, the practical aspects that holds the defendant to his -- to his agreement, to his burden, because if -- if there is no one judging him and his ability to accept his responsibility and to be honest, then the belief is perhaps he won't be as honest as he could be. And Defence counsel want the accused to have that right, to convince you that they're being honest and accepting responsibility. And of course, practically, the Prosecution wants him to know that there is logical consequences to his actions. That's the nature of plea agreements, the nature of the common law adversarial plea agreements. And I know from many discussions over many years that that is something that is not -- that is foreign to the civil law and in fact in many -- many people find it offensive. However, that's why we cite to the Rules and the Chamber -- the Rules, but the request to have the -- the sentence after testimony is basically what I -- what I said, and that's -- if I can answer any other questions on that point, I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think in most of the jurisdictions the commitment itself is part of the agreement. It doesn't depend on the quality of the testimony, whether, you know, the accused is truthful or not to testify against other people or even the co-accused. And we are worried about the credibility of the testimony of this accused without - without - sentencing. We have to be fair to the accused himself as well as to other people the accused will testify against. Another question is: You said you are ready to dismiss the remaining sentence -- the remaining charges in the indictment. Does this mean that the accused pleads guilty to the Prosecution but the other charges are still there against him? Do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is something that is so fundamental that I'm trying to find out -- I'm trying to recall the -- why it works the way it does. But yes, these other charges are basically put on hold. They -- and if the person withdraws his plea for some reason, the charges are there and they're -- the person is reincorporated into the old indictment. But the -- for all intents and purposes, once the Court accepts the -- the guilty plea, those charges are off the books and -- and then they are finally off the books when the Prosecutor -- when the sentence is given and the Prosecutor dismisses them. But once there is a guilty plea accepted by the Court, agreed to by the parties, those charges are put in an off-the-books situation and only to arise again if Defence counsel for some reason withdraws his guilty plea or something else happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the job of this Tribunal is not only to address the personal responsibility of criminal activities but also to safeguard the fundamental rights of the accused. Reading paragraph 17, the waiver of the rights of this agreement, if those charges are still there, at the meantime, the accused waived his right to defend himself, we believe that is a serious violation of this person's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not meant to be that way. It's not, in practice, that way. Counsel doesn't think it's that way. However, the reason that it's a problem in common law is that there's a concern that if these charges are dismissed, they cannot be reinstated. I think we can probably dismiss the charges if -- if you feel that's necessary, as long as they're not dismissed with prejudice and that if, in case something blew up before sentencing, they could be reinstated. That might solve your concerns and solve the traditional concern of why this is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In "the time of the sentencing"; what does this mean? Does it mean that for sentencing specifically for the accused himself, Mr. Nikolic alone, or the sentencing in the entire case? If it's the later case, we have to wait two years?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this means that at the time of Mr. Nikolic's sentencing, as do all the particular elements of this. But perhaps I shouldn't give you an example of how this can work, because I've had cases where people have not been sentenced for two or three years as a very long complicated corruption trial goes on, and that the -- the Trial Chamber wants, and the accused wants, the Court to see this person tell the truth and cooperate in each of the successive trials. And since they know it's a serious crime and the person is going to go to prison for many, many, years, the fact that they go unsentenced for a year or two years is something that both the Prosecution have no problem with nor the accused, because it gives the accused a chance to assist the Prosecution and therefore the value of the Prosecution is higher at the time of sentencing, so the Prosecutor can get up and say, "This witness testified at five Mafia trials and was a truthful witness and a key witness, and as a result the -- he should not face life imprisonment, Your Honour, he should face only," you know, whatever number of years. That's what the accused wants, that's why the accused testifies in five Mafia trials, and that's why he doesn't ask for a sentence before that. The same with the Prosecution. That way, the accused gets the benefit of all that cooperation and all that assistance to law enforcement. It's not considered by either party as any kind of infringement to put it off that long. Now, in this particular case, I would intend to call Mr. Nikolic sometime in June or July, and just as -- as the appropriate timing would allow. And so we wouldn't expect that to be a big burden on -- on anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you going to consider dismissing all the remaining counts at the time that Mr. Nikolic enters a guilty plea to the count, especially to the count 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour, as long as we all understand that it's without prejudice, that if something happens and he withdraws his plea, that those can be reinstated. So that shouldn't be a problem. I think that one we can -- all systems can work around to get a proper ICTY system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any submissions from Defence team concerning paragraph 4 of the plea agreement? What is your understanding of this paragraph, especially of that phrase recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in preparing this agreement, the Defence has understood it just as Mr. McCloskey, my learned friend from the Prosecution has explained it to you. However, if you are concerned about item (b) -- or rather, para (b) of item 4, I endorse Mr. McCloskey's suggestion to solve the problem by having the Prosecution drop other charges against the accused Nikolic when and if you accept his guilty plea on count 5, persecutions, and agree that we leave the possibility to the Prosecution to reactivate either counts if the Defence withdraws its signature from this agreement for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there are some questions asked by Judge Argibay. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: It's addressed to the Prosecution, because I have a practical problem. If you don't drop the counts, you put it on hold, you say, or something like that, in the freezer, let's say, but something comes into the big trial with the other accused related to those counts and related to Mr. Nikolic. How are we going to -- to work with that? Because by this plea agreement he's waiving his right to examine witnesses or to be at the trial, because these counts are out but not out of the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this is something, practically, that each accused knows when they enter a plea agreement, or they're told by their lawyer. And in this particular case, I know this counsel told his client this, that -- tell the whole truth because at the trial and other places, other material comes out, other evidence comes out, and it's very important that when you're finally judged by the Court they see you as telling the truth, so don't hide anything. And so they know that by giving up their right and pleading guilty, they are exposing themselves to evidence as it comes in before the Court and that evidence that may go against them. However, they also have the confidence that at sentencing and in the documents that will be filed in the sentencing both by the Defence and by the Prosecution, that any such issues will be argued by both sides. For example, if something came up in a case that the Prosecution felt was fundamental and was truthful and was not as the person in -- that made the plea agreement said, then at sentencing the Prosecution is free, under this agreement, to tell you that the -- that the person did not cooperate as fully as we had anticipated. And however, if that same information that comes out of trial is something that we believe was fabricated, we would at sentencing say, "We do not believe that information involving the accused is true and that it should not affect his overall cooperation." So you would be hearing from both sides on such material, and you would have a chance to evaluate what both sides said about it as well as question the defendant on that point. But yes, you would not have the chance to have counsel cross-examine at the trial that various evidence. That's given up when the person pleads guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very clear yet about that, but then I'll turn to another thing. The question is, from my point of view, that the -- the accused is waiving a lot of rights and the counterpart, it's not very equal to that if you're not going to drop the charges, the other counts. That means that he's waiving all his right, even the right to be considered innocent until convicted, at least in one charge, for one charge. And he's not getting, on the other side, the same waiver of rights. For instance, the right to reinstate the charges should be dropped, in my -- from my point of view. Don't you think that you must keep a sort of balance between the two parties and it's not very fair to ask the accused to waive all of his rights and not giving him at least this security on dropping the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There -- the simple -- there is a simple answer to that question. In effect, this plea agreement drops those other charges. They're gone. And they're almost never reinstated. The only time that one tries to reinstate them is, like I said, when the plea is withdrawn. And so it's not a problem for the Prosecution to dismiss those charges today, and we'll just -- as long as they're not done under prejudice. You see, in the -- when charges are dismissed by prosecutors where I come from, many times they can never been charged again. It's over. It's an inflexible system in some respects, much less flexible than the civil law system, and so that is why that particular odd -- setting the charges in the freezer is there. But I think, practically, we can dismiss those charges today and not have any problem from anyone. I think we have an agreement, those charges are gone, and it shouldn't be a problem. Now, I can mention to you briefly what I think the Prosecution is giving up in this agreement, because I believe they're giving up a lot, but I think there's a lot of good reasons to do it. And I can also tell you that but I don't know if perhaps you want to hear that tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The next set of questions concerning of the paragraph 5 of the plea agreement, which is related to paragraph 31 of the indictment. The plea agreement suggests that deletion of the phrase "genocide -- complicity in genocide" and "murder as a violation of the laws or customs of wars" in paragraph 31 of the indictment. However, the phrase "crimes against humanity, including murder, persecution, forcible transfer, and inhuman acts," remains in this paragraph. There are several issues I would like to seek some clarifications from the Prosecution: Whether this deletion is related to the particular accused, that is, Mr. Nikolic, or to all the persons listed in this indictment, because in the chapeau, in the first paragraph we have four names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This agreement is only meant to affect Mr. Nikolic. And on your particular point, this afternoon Mr. Waespi pointed out to me that these -- the other murder and crimes against humanity were counts that were actually being dismissed and that those should be cut out also. When we left them in, we thought they were part of the umbrella of persecutions, because as you know, persecutions use the same terminology. But then as I looked at that again just recently, I realised no, it has to do with the other charged counts, and yes, those should be deleted as well. That's -- Mr. Waespi and I had a debate on it but I think I know how it should be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you answered my second question instead of the first one. My second question is that the accused only pleads to Article 5(H), that is, the persecution. But, however, the remaining phrase in paragraph 31 indicates other crimes against humanity, such as murder, forcible transfer, and inhuman acts in addition to that of the persecution as a crime against humanity. I think you somehow answered this question, you know. But my question is that: In the chapeau or in the first sentence of this paragraph, there are four accused named as committing such kind of crimes. So this deletion is applicable only to the accused, that is, Mr. Nikolic himself, alone, or to all the four accused in this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, only -- only Mr. Nikolic alone. That language stays for all the rest, because they have chosen to go to trial on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next question is concerning with the paragraph 5.3. It says: "Paragraph 45 (second subparagraph, third sentence): Instead of 'in compliance with the orders of Mr. Blagojevic,' it should say 'under the authority of Mr. Blagojevic.'" This change or amendment of the indictment concerning another person, another accused, I wonder if it's proper to change any contents of the indictment without the presence and the knowledge of that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this was just identified as the correct way to factually and legally view this, and this plea agreement and its changes have been sent to all Defence, so they have been put on notice of this -- of this change. And in fact, the change benefits Mr. Blagojevic because at first we thought there was an order and then, going over the facts with Mr. Nikolic, it was determined that he was acting under the authority of his commander but not under direct orders. So we felt it would be important to clear that up legally first in this document for Mr. Nikolic but then, as soon as we get a little breathing space, present to you an amended indictment for the other accused, leaving off Mr. Nikolic and fixing this change. We also just found another typo in the indictment which we would fix also. And so in that event, counsel have been notified, and it is to their benefit, and we fully intend to do that and correct it. But it was, of course, something we didn't learn until the last day or two, as we had discussions with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I also hope that the Defence counsel and Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic will think along your way, but at least I think Mr. Blagojevic should be given the notice of this suggested change to the indictment. And in case of objections, it might impact his case adversely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This has been sent today to counsel for Mr. Blagojevic. And the actual motion to amend the indictment, to fix it, will give Mr. Blagojevic and anyone else a chance to challenge any changes and litigate that issue. And so I -- I think that that is well -- well taken care of and that we have acted timely and we're trying to get at the truth and be as accurate as we can as events unfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any submissions from the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, the next set of questions are concerning with paragraph 9 to 11 of the plea agreement; namely, cooperation by Mr. Nikolic. In the paragraph 9, the agreement is contingent upon Mr. Nikolic's acceptance of the responsibility and the decision to cooperate with the OTP whenever requested. What does it mean by "contingent upon"? Do the parties mean contingency upon or based on? We need some clarifications on that word. Maybe Mr. McCloskey could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Basically, Mr. Nikolic is promising to cooperate with us, meaning, as we state, he's agreeing to meet with us when we can, go over the facts with us, and testify truthfully and provide us the truth. And if he does that, the continue -- the agreement stays in force, and at the time of sentencing he will bear the benefit of his agreement, and we will so tell the Court that he is able to do that. However, if in a situation like this an accused decided he didn't want to speak with the Prosecution any more or didn't want to testify any more, that -- then he would be in breach of this agreement and the Prosecution would not be bound by its promises, which are the recommendation of the 15 to 20 years. It's an agreement for him to cooperate and tell the truth and that we provide our sentencing agreement based on that cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And now, what points do you consider that Mr. Nikolic has fulfilled his obligations and the agreement will take effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Practically, this works at the -- at the time of his sentencing, where it's fully evaluated, his -- his ability to meet with us, tell us the truth, his ability to truthfully testify at trial, his ability to accept his responsibility, and then once -- once the sentence is sent, after he's had a chance to show you that and cooperate with the Prosecution, then he will bear the benefit of that agreement and be sentenced as a result of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Does that mean that this agreement will take effect after his signing of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, it's meant to take effect upon his signing. I would expect that if we needed to speak to him in the next few days, that he would, based on his agreement, speak to us, and I'm sure he would. So the agreement is in effect at the signing. He agrees to continue to cooperate; we agree to tell you about that cooperation so you can evaluate it in relation to the appropriate sentence. Of course, it's just one factor in sentencing, cooperation, but as you know, it's an important one because how important it is to save the Tribunal time and to have people step up and take responsibility, it is only one factor. Of course the nature of the crime, the events, everything else, is -- is also part of the sentencing, but this is just one -- one important factor. And this ability to let you see him cooperate and tell the truth is one of the biggest values he has to himself and to this Tribunal. That's why sentencing should be after you have a chance to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, you use terminology as "the upcoming trial." What do you mean by that? Does it mean only the trial of the three other accused in that case or the trial, if you do not drop the other charges, do you mean the trial still against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- we meant -- "the upcoming trial," we meant this trial, and we can be more specific on that, but that's -- that's the one that is hovering over all of us, so there was no -- for us, there was no issue of which one it was, but we can be more specific. And if you accept this plea, I will dismiss those other charges today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are still, you know, wondering what is the criteria for the -- for the accused to testify as truthful and candid, and how is that measured and enforced? What's the criteria for you to judge whether the accused give truthful testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's most important for you to make that determination, based on all you know about the case, be it from the written record or the -- in this case there may be a trial. And we'll basically be doing the same thing you are; we'll be going on our knowledge of the written investigation and what other people say and our knowledge of the case to determine whether we believe he is in fact telling the truth or -- and cooperating in meeting his side of the burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you mean that you will not decide that, you know, arbitrarily, or by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do make that decision ourselves. We do not make it arbitrarily. But it is the Judges' prerogative in the end to make that decision. We will make our recommendations to you, but it is, of course, your discretion to decide whether you believe he is cooperating, based on what we say, what Defence says, what you see him do in court; everything before you. But that's -- that is principally your responsibility and -- but we will hopefully help you with that, based on our knowledge of the case and -- and what we -- what we -- you know, seven years of the investigation and watching him testify. So I think we can add to that and be helpful. But fundamentally you're the most important arbiters of that -- of that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When do you expect the accused to testify in that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Prior to the summer break. June or July, I would hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any submissions from the Defence team or any observations concerning with those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused Nikolic agreed to testify, to tell the truth, and to cooperate with the Prosecution in the belief that in that way he will achieve significant cooperation, which under the Rules - and I'm sure you are familiar with that - is the only mitigating circumstance under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mr. Nikolic, assuming -- on assuming his responsibility and guilt, is prepared to also assume responsibility, and in assuming this responsibility, he's prepared to tell the truth. He has promised that he will tell the truth, that he will not lie at all. He's prepared to cooperate with the Prosecution in order to achieve this cooperation and so that he could receive a recommendation by the Prosecution during the sentencing that he sincerely and honestly cooperated with the Prosecution. And I hope that we will come to this point and that this will have an effect on the severity of the sentence that will be passed down. And I completely agree with all that Mr. McCloskey has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The next set of questions concerning with paragraphs 17 and 18, which is about the waiver of the rights of the accused that we have already been touched upon. But we believe that those conditions are very strict. There are some fundamental rights that the accused should not be deprived of. For instance, the right not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilty, the right to be tried without undue delay, the right to testify or to remain silent at trial. Based on what circumstances those conditions, those waiver, were drafted? We would like to know some background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, when an accused voluntarily decides to plead guilty, he is waiving his right to remain silent because he is standing up and saying, "I am guilty." So by definition, he's waiving his right to remain silent and he is gaining a great benefit in doing so because he's accepting responsibility, and as Mr. Londrovic said, he hopes to be benefitted that by you. So he has to set aside his right to remain silent in order to stand and tell you, and tell the world, that he accepts responsibility for this. There's no way to do that without saying -- standing -- setting aside his right to remain silent. The -- for the other two rights you mentioned, the same thing applies. By doing that, he has to set aside those rights, just by his very act that will benefit him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, some of the rights listed here are so fundamental, I, of course -- you know, maybe that is a theoretical issue, but we believe that some of the rights is inalienable, is not deprived of, not by anybody, some of them even by himself. But that's -- that's another matter. Yes. Another question is concerning of the paragraph 18, that "the accused does not waive his right to be represented by Counsel at all stages of the proceedings." What do you mean by "the proceedings"? It means the proceedings in the sentencing proceedings of this particular accused or the proceedings of the case with the three accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It means the sentencing proceedings, or perhaps when he testifies, counsel would like to be present while he was testifying. Sometimes counsel does like to be present. And any other court proceedings or any other time that he needs his counsel. This is just designed to let him know that he always has his counsel, that while in order to plead guilty and agree to testify you're waiving your fundamental rights, you never ever waive your right to have counsel. And that's -- that paragraph is there for the very purpose that I think concerned you in the previous one. There are certain things that should never been waived. And again, we do get into philosophical arguments and the view of the individual and his rights, but that's probably for another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any submissions from Defence team, or any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is all the questions, you know, concerning with this plea agreement. I must confess that we do not have enough time to study it. And by reading this plea agreement, we understand it's -- it was drafted in a hasty manner and that there's something to be corrected and amended. I hope, after this hearing, that both parties will get together, while taking into consideration of the observations made by this Trial Chamber, they'll try to work out a presentable agreement. We are ready to entertain it whenever you are ready. Is that agreeable, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will try to reassess, based on your -- your comments. However, I would like to tell you this was not done hastily. This was done in great consideration. We spent a lot of time and we carefully went over each paragraph of the indictment. We have spent hours and hours and hours together, all of us. We've taken this responsibility very gravely. And I can see the -- one of your main concerns is -- I can dismiss the other counts and get -- though, frankly, I -- and we will try to see if there are other significant concerns, but -- and we will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, my question relates to the para 17. Do you mean that Mr. Nikolic is giving up his rights in relation to all charges or only to the charges dismissed by para 4(b)?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Practically, he's giving up his rights for all charges and the charges that are put in the freezer as well. But we can get around that problem by putting those charges elsewhere, so they're gone. So I think we can solve that one very simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you mean that the Bench can ask the accused the questions and the accused had obligation to answer these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. Once he pleads guilty, it's required of the Court - and counsel and the accused know this - that you be satisfied that there's a factual basis for this charge, and questions from the Court are absolutely appropriate in that context, and I am sure Mr. Nikolic and his counsel are prepared to answer any questions you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any comments and submissions from Defence team? Are you agreeable with this solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I hope both parties could get together to go over the whole plea agreement. And as I said, that we are ready to entertain it at any time when you are ready. So the hearing is adjourned.
